nodes.label: Chapter 7 Wireless and Mobile Networks
nodes.rationale: Kurose and Ross 9th edition slides (Pearson, 2025) covering radio, wireless access, the 5G core, mobility, Bluetooth, satellite, and IoT.

nodes.label: Wireless Host
nodes.rationale: A laptop, smartphone, or IoT device that runs applications and may be stationary or mobile; wireless connectivity does not imply mobility.

nodes.label: Base Station
nodes.rationale: Typically wired to the infrastructure and relays packets between the wired network and wireless hosts in its area, such as a 4G/5G cell tower or an 802.11 access point.

nodes.label: WiFi Access Point
nodes.rationale: The 802.11 base station that bridges wireless hosts to an institutional wired network and the Internet.

nodes.label: Ad Hoc Network
nodes.rationale: A wireless network with no infrastructure such as an access point or base station; devices must organize the network themselves.

nodes.label: Path Loss
nodes.rationale: Radio power falls with frequency and distance, roughly (fd)^n, with n about 2 in free space, 2.7-3.5 in urban settings, and 3-6 indoors.

nodes.label: Hidden Terminal Problem
nodes.rationale: Path loss and obstacles let A hear B and B hear C while A and C cannot hear each other, so they collide at B without knowing it.

nodes.label: Multipath Propagation
nodes.rationale: Reflections off the ground and buildings arrive at slightly different times than the line-of-sight path; coherence time shrinks as frequency and receiver speed rise.

nodes.label: MIMO
nodes.rationale: Multiple-input multiple-output antennas provide spatial diversity (redundant streams for reliability and range) or spatial multiplexing (independent streams), and multi-user MIMO uses beamforming toward separated users.

nodes.label: Signal-to-Noise Ratio
nodes.rationale: SNR in dB is 10 log10 of received signal power over noise power. The slides cite a cellular lower limit around -10 to -6 dB and a WiFi lower limit around 20 dB.

nodes.label: Shannon Capacity
nodes.rationale: C = B log2(1 + SNR) is the maximum rate given bandwidth and SNR. Capacity scales linearly with bandwidth and only logarithmically with high SNR.

nodes.label: Shannon 1948 Paper
nodes.rationale: The slides attribute the channel-capacity result to Shannon's classic 1948 paper, without a full bibliographic citation.

nodes.label: Quadrature Amplitude Modulation
nodes.rationale: m-QAM encodes log2(m) bits in amplitude and phase. The slides show 4-QAM, 16-QAM, and 64-QAM constellations used by WiFi, generalizing QPSK.

nodes.label: Adaptive Modulation
nodes.rationale: As interference and transmit power change SNR, the sender switches modulation and power to the highest rate that still meets an acceptable bit-error rate and energy cost.

nodes.label: OFDM
nodes.rationale: Orthogonal frequency-division multiplexing packs overlapping subcarriers so crosstalk cancels at each subcarrier center, avoiding the guard bands of plain FDM.

nodes.label: OFDMA
nodes.rationale: OFDMA assigns time-frequency resource blocks to users. The slides list it for 4G/5G, WiFi 6, Bluetooth, and satellite.

nodes.label: Resource Block
nodes.rationale: The smallest scheduling unit assigned to one user. In 4G a resource block is 84 symbols (12 subcarriers by 7 symbols); the base station reassigns blocks about every 1 ms.

nodes.label: CSMA/CA
nodes.rationale: 802.11 sends the whole frame after the channel is idle for DIFS, with no collision detection. The receiver returns an ACK after SIFS because a hidden terminal may have corrupted the frame, and the backoff doubles after a missing ACK.

nodes.label: RTS/CTS
nodes.rationale: A short request-to-send reserves the medium; the base station broadcasts clear-to-send with the duration so every station that hears either frame defers. WiFi 6/7 extends this with multiuser RTS before OFDMA.

nodes.label: IEEE 802.11
nodes.rationale: The wireless LAN link-layer standard. Frames carry up to four MAC addresses, a duration field for RTS/CTS, and type bits for management, control, and data.

nodes.label: WiFi 6
nodes.rationale: 802.11ax (2020) is WiFi 6, with a theoretical 9.5 Gbps on 2.4 and 5 GHz using OFDM, OFDMA, and MIMO. WiFi 7 (802.11be, 2024) adds 6 GHz and 320 MHz channels.

nodes.label: 4G LTE
nodes.rationale: 4G LTE uses OFDMA with 15 kHz subcarriers and a maximum carrier bandwidth of 20 MHz. Its base station is the eNodeB and its mobility anchor in the older architecture is the MME.

nodes.label: 5G New Radio
nodes.rationale: 5G NR keeps OFDMA but allows 15, 30, 60, or 120 kHz subcarriers and up to 100 MHz carrier bandwidth. Low, mid, and high (mmWave) bands trade range for rate.

nodes.label: gNodeB
nodes.rationale: The 5G base station (Next Generation Node B) is the single base station in a RAN and the first-hop relay between user equipment and the mobile core.

nodes.label: User Equipment
nodes.rationale: The 5G mobile device. All of its packets pass through the base station, and it reports channel quality and sends scheduling requests on the uplink control channel.

nodes.label: 5G Core Network
nodes.rationale: One core serves many RANs. It is an all-IP core whose services differ from ordinary Internet applications, and most of its specified functions are control-plane services.

nodes.label: Control and User Plane Separation
nodes.rationale: CUPS splits 5G control-plane functions and services from the user-plane forwarding path, with well-defined interfaces such as N1, N2, N3, and N4 between them.

nodes.label: User Plane Function
nodes.rationale: Each device is assigned a UPF that relays traffic to the Internet and enforces policy, lawful intercept, usage measurement, and QoS. It also tunnels traffic to the base station over N3.

nodes.label: Access and Mobility Management Function
nodes.rationale: AMF handles connection and reachability, mobility, access authorization, and location services, and is the key function when a device registers.

nodes.label: Session Management Function
nodes.rationale: SMF manages each UE session: IP address allocation, UPF selection, QoS control, and the control aspects of user-plane routing.

nodes.label: GTP-U
nodes.rationale: On the N3 backhaul, the user IP packet is carried inside GTP-U over UDP/IP between the UPF and the base station.

nodes.label: Radio Resource Control
nodes.rationale: RRC configures coarse policy for the RAN pipeline, including scheduling priority and security. It is the control plane and does not process user-plane packets.

nodes.label: Packet Data Convergence Protocol
nodes.rationale: PDCP compresses IP headers and provides ciphering and integrity protection on the RAN user-plane path above RLC, MAC, and PHY.

nodes.label: O-RAN
nodes.rationale: O-RAN splits a formerly monolithic base station into a Central Unit, Distributed Unit, and Radio Unit; where each unit runs is an implementation choice.

nodes.label: Software-Defined RAN
nodes.rationale: SD-RAN refactors RRC into a control-plane proxy and a Real-Time Intelligent Controller. Near-real-time xApps such as load balancing, handover, and QoS share a RAN Network Information Base.

nodes.label: 5G Handover
nodes.rationale: The device changes its point of attachment when the target base station has a stronger signal or less load. The source station forwards data until the SMF points the UPF tunnel at the target.

nodes.label: Extended Service Set
nodes.rationale: 802.11 treats mobility as a link-layer problem: several basic service sets share one SSID and one layer-3 subnet, with fast re-authentication between them.

nodes.label: Bluetooth
nodes.rationale: An ad hoc cable-replacement architecture with its own stack, not the Internet stack. Classic Bluetooth has no network or transport layer and no routing.

nodes.label: Bluetooth Low Energy
nodes.rationale: BLE uses 2 MHz channels (40 total: 3 advertising and 37 data) and, unlike Classic Bluetooth, adds managed flooding. It has a separate controller from Classic Bluetooth.

nodes.label: Bluetooth Piconet
nodes.rationale: A piconet is generally under 10 m and has at most eight devices: one central and up to seven peripherals. Peripherals talk only to the central, which polls them for channel access.

nodes.label: L2CAP
nodes.rationale: Logical Link Control and Adaptation creates end-to-end channels with reliability, flow control, and segmentation: connection-oriented ACL, connectionless ACL, or synchronous eSCO for audio.

nodes.label: Bluetooth Frequency Hopping
nodes.rationale: A piconet hops among 79 channels, one frequency per 625 microsecond slot, so an interferer on one ISM channel hits only an occasional slot and the frame is retried on another frequency.

nodes.label: Low Earth Orbit Satellite
nodes.rationale: LEO satellites orbit at 550-1200 km, move about 27,000 km/h, stay in line of sight for 5-15 minutes, and have about 30 ms RTT. Wide coverage needs a constellation and inter-satellite links.

nodes.label: Geosynchronous Satellite
nodes.rationale: A GEO satellite is stationary relative to the ground at 35,768 km, covers a wide area, and has about 800 ms RTT.

nodes.label: Starlink
nodes.rationale: The slides (April 2025) describe about 7,239 operational Starlink LEO satellites in shells at 525, 530, and 535 km, with Internet service and planned inter-satellite links.

nodes.label: Inter-Satellite Link
nodes.rationale: Links between LEO satellites turn a constellation into a network in the sky, with routing across multiple satellite hops rather than a single bent-pipe hop.

nodes.label: Bent-Pipe Satellite Architecture
nodes.rationale: A bent pipe is a single satellite hop between base stations, so the satellite is a link in the sky rather than a router.

nodes.label: Internet of Things
nodes.rationale: IoT spans meters to kilometers, from hundreds of bits per second for metering up to about 1 Mbps for video, and energy is always a constraint, including devices that run about 10 years without external power.

nodes.label: LoRaWAN
nodes.rationale: Named with LTE-M as a low-power wide-area option, distinct from short-range WiFi, BLE, and Zigbee and from traditional 4G/5G cellular.

nodes.label: Zigbee
nodes.rationale: A short-range IoT radio that shares the unlicensed 2.4 GHz ISM band with WiFi, Bluetooth, and many other consumer devices.

nodes.label: Discontinuous Reception
nodes.rationale: After an inactivity timer the device enters short DRX, then long DRX. Longer sleep saves energy but adds latency and can affect TCP, and the base station buffers downlink packets until the device wakes.

nodes.label: Proportional Fairness Scheduling
nodes.rationale: PF picks the user and resource block that maximize expected rate over recent achieved rate, combining maximum-throughput scheduling with blind equal throughput. Standards leave this choice to the operator.

nodes.label: Subscriber Identity Module
nodes.rationale: A SIM or vSIM identifies the subscriber and home network to cellular networks worldwide and holds cryptographic key material also known to the home network.

nodes.label: Channel Quality Indicator
nodes.rationale: The UE measures reference signals and reports a 4-bit CQI that maps to the modulation, such as which QAM, and the expected throughput the scheduler should assume.

nodes.label: Unlicensed Spectrum
nodes.rationale: Unlicensed bands are open to anyone who follows power rules. The slides name 2.4 GHz and 5 GHz WiFi and 3.5 GHz CBRS (private 5G), in contrast to licensed cellular spectrum sold by auction.
